catalog_change_requests.detail: There is no serum cortisol, random cortisol, ACTH or cosyntropin stimulation entry in the catalog. The case therefore cannot let a resident confirm the adrenal diagnosis with the test they would actually send, and the diagnosis must be made entirely on the pattern of sodium, potassium, glucose and catecholamine-resistant shock. That is defensible teaching, because treatment does precede confirmation in a suspected crisis and a cortisol assay would not return inside a real emergency department resuscitation either. It is still a gap: a resident who orders the right test should be told it has been sent and will not return, not find that the test does not exist.

The catalog's coagulation panel carries PT, INR and aPTT, and there is no fibrinogen orderable. The seed specifies fibrinogen as a key value that starts normal or high and falls, which is the finding that distinguishes early from established consumptive coagulopathy. It is authored here as a fourth component of the coagulation panel payload. This works, and it means the case's panel has a component the catalog default does not, which a reviewer should confirm is acceptable rather than a schema violation.

The catalog offers D50 and D5, with nothing between them. Ten percent dextrose titrated to effect is increasingly the preferred treatment for hypoglycaemia in an alert patient, and it cannot be selected.

The case author asked for a Notify Public Health action to be added to the Consults tab. It already exists: consult_public_health_authorities, in the consultations tab, with state_changing_overridable set true. No catalog change is required. This case overrides it to state_changing and has it set a flag, which is what the overridable marker is for.

metadata.working_title: Twenty-one year old woman, fever and a rash on her ankles, brought in by EMS
metadata.chief_complaint_patient_voice: Everything hurts and I can't stop shaking.
metadata.final_diagnosis: Invasive meningococcal disease: Neisseria meningitidis bacteraemia (meningococcaemia) with septic shock, early disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury, and acute primary adrenal insufficiency from bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome). No meningitis.
learning_objectives: Treat fever plus a non-blanching petechial rash plus shock as invasive meningococcal disease until proven otherwise, and start antibiotics on that clinical picture rather than on a confirmatory test.

Recognise the biochemical signature of acute primary adrenal insufficiency sitting inside a septic presentation: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia together, with shock that does not settle on volume alone. Give hydrocortisone, not dextrose alone.
Sequence the resuscitation: cultures if they do not delay, antibiotics immediately, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, then norepinephrine for hypotension that persists after volume.
State when the lumbar puncture must wait. Haemodynamic instability and coagulopathy are both contraindications to positioning, and antibiotics are never delayed for cerebrospinal fluid.

Carry out the public health duties of a notifiable disease: droplet precautions, personal protective equipment, notification on suspicion rather than on culture, and chemoprophylaxis for close contacts.
Read a disseminated intravascular coagulation panel as a description of the sepsis rather than as an order set for blood products or anticoagulation.
metadata.teaching_frame: Deliberately the stereotypical presentation of invasive meningococcal disease in a college-age patient, with one layer added: the shock has two causes running at once. The intent is pattern consolidation plus the specific recognition that catecholamine-resistant shock with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in fulminant sepsis is adrenal, and that hydrocortisone is a separate critical action from the antibiotic.

care_setting.label: Quaternary care, Level 1 trauma centre
care_setting.detail: Adult emergency department. Full laboratory, imaging and blood bank on site. Critical care, infectious diseases, nephrology and haematology available in house at all hours. The hospital laboratory does not offer a random serum cortisol or ACTH with a turnaround that would return inside this encounter, which matches the catalog: neither test exists as an orderable. Nothing else in this case is limited by resources.
care_setting.provenance: Setting is a deployment property, not a clinical fact.

arrival.line: Brought in by EMS. Handover given on arrival in the resuscitation bay.

metadata.complaint: Fever and a rash on her ankles

patient.background: No past medical history. No regular medications other than a combined oral contraceptive pill, which she takes irregularly. No allergies. No previous surgery. Second-year university student living in a shared hall of residence. Received the routine adolescent meningococcal conjugate vaccine at 11 and a booster at 16; never received a serogroup B vaccine, which in the United States is offered on shared clinical decision-making rather than routinely. Never smoked, drinks socially at weekends, no illicit drug use. Last menstrual period two weeks ago, uses pads rather than tampons.
patient.presenting_vitals_source: Inherited from phase 'presentation'. EMS established a single 20 gauge cannula in the left hand and gave nothing en route.
patient.presenting_appearance: A young woman lying curled on her side on the stretcher, shivering intermittently, pale and sweating, answering questions correctly but slowly and asking to be left alone. She keeps reaching for her thighs and calves. Dark spots are visible on both ankles and the dorsum of each foot.
patient.ems_handover_text: Twenty-one year old, roommate rang us this morning. Fever since last night, been vomiting, said her legs were too painful to stand on. Roommate says she has not been making much sense for the last hour or so. There is a rash on her ankles that was not there yesterday. We have a small line in the back of her left hand. Nothing given.
patient.arrival_handover: Twenty-one year old, her roommate called us, she's been running a fever since last night and she's been really out of it this morning. Complaining her legs are killing her, and there's a rash come up on her ankles.
patient.arrival_handover_authoring_note: Two sentences, 39 words, no vital signs, no past history, no medication, no allergy, no pertinent negative, no word naming a diagnosis. Deliberately imprecise in one respect: 'really out of it' overstates a patient who is GCS 15 on arrival, which is the kind of error a crew actually makes. The rash is mentioned because a crew would mention it and because it is visible on the skin examination anyway; withholding it would be artificial rather than difficult.

phase_notes.count_justification: Six clinical phases plus two terminal phases. Section 3.3 of the authoring requirements asks for three to six clinical phases, so this case sits exactly at the ceiling. The six are forced by the seed, which specifies two independent deficits (glucocorticoid and antimicrobial) and therefore two distinct failure branches, plus two distinct resolution states depending on whether a vasopressor was ever needed.
phase_notes.deterioration_paths: Two branches. 'adrenal_crisis' is entered by resuscitating volume or glucose without replacing glucocorticoid, and 'progressive_meningococcaemia' by replacing glucocorticoid without treating the organism. Both are recoverable and both have an exit action that exists in the catalog: hydrocortisone and a third-generation cephalosporin respectively.
phase_notes.engine_limitation_on_state_4: RESOLVED in v0.6. The seed specifies that state 4 is reached by continued progression despite delayed treatment. Until v0.6 the engine had no time-driven transitions and this phase was reachable only by intubating, which misattributed the deterioration to an action the resident took rather than to one they omitted. It is now reachable both ways: by intubation, which remains clinically real, and by the clock at 210 seconds from either deterioration branch. See the deterioration timeline artifact.
phase_notes.time_guarded_transitions: Five, listed in the deterioration timeline. Two out of the presentation phase at 240 seconds, one for the unreplaced glucocorticoid and one for the untreated organism, ordered so that a patient who has had neither enters the adrenal branch first, which matches the seed's ordering of states 2 and 3 and keeps the progressive phase's laboratory values, which assume glucocorticoid replacement, internally consistent. One out of each deterioration branch at 210 seconds into frank septic shock. One out of frank septic shock at 300 seconds into cardiac arrest, which is terminal and carries the explicit opt-in. A completely passive resident arrests at 750 seconds against an estimated runtime of 600.

phases.label: Compensated septic shock with occult adrenal insufficiency
phases.clinical_description: Febrile, tachycardic, peripherally shut down with a non-blanching petechial rash and a normal blood pressure. Hyponatraemic, hyperkalaemic and hypoglycaemic. Alert. The compensation is still holding.

transitions.author_note: Induction and positive pressure in vasoplegic, volume-depleted, glucocorticoid-deficient shock. Modelled as certain here for teaching.

transitions.when: flag abx_given set AND flag steroid_given set AND flag fluids_given set
transitions.author_note: All three deficits addressed: organism, cortisol, volume.

transitions.when: flag fluids_given set AND flag steroid_given set
transitions.author_note: Volume and cortisol replaced, organism untreated.
Volume given, glucocorticoid deficit uncorrected. Seed state 2.
Dextrose without hydrocortisone is the seed's other named route into state 2. The glucose falls again.

transitions.narration: She's harder to rouse than she was ten minutes ago, doctor, and she's gone a worse colour. Her pressure's come down too. I don't think she's holding.
transitions.debrief_note: The glucocorticoid deficit was never addressed and the crisis progressed on its own. This is the part of the illness that does not wait for you. Nothing in the first four minutes required a laboratory result: a previously well 21 year old who is shocked, peripherally shut down and hypoglycaemic has an adrenal problem until proven otherwise, and hydrocortisone is given on that suspicion.
transitions.author_rationale: Untreated acute adrenal insufficiency progresses over minutes to hours. Ordered above the antibiotic timer so that a patient who has had neither drug enters the adrenal branch first, which matches the seed's ordering of states 2 and 3 and keeps the progressive phase's laboratory values, which assume glucocorticoid replacement, internally consistent.

transitions.narration: The spots on her ankles have joined up into patches while we've been standing here, and there are new ones on her forearms. She's oozing round the cannula site now too.
transitions.debrief_note: The organism was never treated and the septicaemia progressed. Meningococcal disease is measured in hours and the rash is the clock you can see. Antibiotics are given on the clinical picture, not on a culture, an antigen test or a lumbar puncture.
transitions.author_rationale: Untreated meningococcal bacteraemia progresses. Reachable only when glucocorticoid has been replaced, because the rule above it catches every patient who has not had it.

phases.label: Progressive adrenal crisis
phases.clinical_description: Resuscitated with volume or glucose but not with glucocorticoid. Hypotensive, more lethargic, glucose falling again, potassium and sodium worse. Seed state 2.

transitions.when: flag steroid_given set AND flag abx_given set

transitions.narration: Her pressure's in the seventies now and she's not answering me properly. I can't feel a radial pulse on either side.
transitions.debrief_note: This is the phase the seed calls frank septic shock, and it was reached by the clock rather than by anything you did. The patient was already in adrenal crisis and the glucocorticoid was never given. Volume and catecholamines both work poorly without cortisol, which is why the shock kept deepening while she was being resuscitated.
transitions.author_rationale: Progression of an untreated adrenal crisis into refractory shock. Shorter than the presentation timer because she is already further along.

phases.label: Progressive meningococcaemia with worsening disseminated intravascular coagulation
phases.clinical_description: Glucocorticoid replaced and volume given, but the organism is untreated. Hypotensive, oliguric, petechiae now coalescing into purpura, platelets and fibrinogen falling. Seed state 3.

transitions.when: flag abx_given set AND flag pressor_running set

transitions.narration: The purpura is spreading up both legs and onto her belly, and she's stopped answering me. Her pressure is seventy over forty.
transitions.debrief_note: The organism was never treated and the septicaemia progressed to refractory shock. Hydrocortisone treated the adrenal failure that the infection caused; it does nothing to the infection. The two deficits need two drugs.

phases.label: Frank septic shock after intubation
phases.clinical_description: Induction agent vasodilation and positive pressure ventilation on top of vasoplegia, volume depletion and glucocorticoid deficiency. Mean arterial pressure below 60, obtunded, purpura expanding, lactate above 5. Seed state 4.

transitions.when: flag abx_given set AND flag steroid_given set AND flag pressor_running set
transitions.author_note: The seed's rescue: antibiotics, hydrocortisone, crystalloid and norepinephrine together.

transitions.when: NOT (flag abx_given set AND flag steroid_given set AND flag pressor_running set)
transitions.narration: She's lost her output. No pulse. I'm starting compressions.
transitions.debrief_note: She arrested. All three deficits were still open: the organism, the cortisol and the perfusion pressure. This is the only phase in this case that the clock can end, and it requires five minutes of refractory shock with none of the three treated. The point is not that you were slow; it is that the case had told you what was missing, through the chemistry panel, the rash and the nurse, and none of the three was ever given.
transitions.author_rationale: Untreated fulminant meningococcaemia with adrenal crisis has a case fatality far above the 10 to 15 percent quoted for treated invasive meningococcal disease, and death within hours of presentation is the characteristic course. Authored as a terminal time-driven transition, which requires the explicit opt-in below. This is the single decision in this case most in need of a physician's sign-off: see the review packet.
transitions.terminal_opt_in_rationale: Death by clock is otherwise forbidden by the validator. It is authored here because the seed specifies progression toward peri-arrest on failure to intervene, because the disease genuinely does this, and because every one of the three required actions has a nurse prompt firing well before the deadline.

phases.label: Responding to antibiotics, hydrocortisone and volume
phases.clinical_description: Resolution phase. Perfusion restored without a vasopressor, glucose stable, mentation clear, rash no longer extending. Still critically ill and still needs intensive care. Seed state 1.

phases.label: Stabilised septic shock on norepinephrine
phases.clinical_description: Resolution phase for the path that required vasopressor support. Mean arterial pressure 65 to 70 on norepinephrine, lactate clearing, urine output returning, vasopressor-dependent. Seed state 5.

phases.label: Cardiac arrest from untreated septic and adrenal shock
phases.clinical_description: Terminal phase entered by the clock, not by an action, after five minutes of refractory shock with the organism, the cortisol and the perfusion pressure all still untreated.
phases.timeout_reason: Five minutes passed in refractory septic shock with no antibiotic, no glucocorticoid and no vasopressor. Perfusion pressure fell below the level that sustains the coronary circulation and she lost cardiac output.
phases.authoring_note: A separate terminal phase rather than the shared 'halted' phase, because 'halted' carries a harmful action's halt reason and this was not a harmful action. Content keys are not authored for this phase, for the same reason they are not authored for 'halted': the case has ended and nothing is queryable. The general status line is authored anyway, since it is the one thing the debrief renders.
phases.vitals_note: The last values the monitor showed before output was lost, not a measurement taken during the arrest. This follows the convention the halted phase already uses: the schema requires a plausible number per phase and a terminal phase has no blood pressure to report.

phases.label: Case halted after a harmful action
phases.clinical_description: Terminal phase entered directly when a harmful action is taken, carrying that action's halt reason. Not reached through transition rules.
phases.schema_gap_note: One vitals block per phase, but the harmful actions in this case produce different physiology: beta blockade produces bradycardic collapse, insulin produces a hypoglycaemic arrest with a normal rate until late. These are generic peri-arrest values. Per-halt vitals would need a schema change; flagged in the review packet.

phases.label: Handoff confirmed
phases.clinical_description: Terminal phase entered when the resident confirms a handoff. The debrief is generated from here.
phases.schema_gap_note: Vitals here are a placeholder copied from 'improving'. The completion phase should inherit the vitals of the phase the resident handed off from, which the current schema cannot express. Same gap the reference case recorded.

tag.when: phase is presentation

case_actions.debrief_note: Rate limiting and unglamorous. Every drug that matters in this case is intravenous: the cephalosporin, the hydrocortisone, the crystalloid, the dextrose and the vasopressor. A resident who orders all five before anyone has a line has ordered five things that cannot happen. Two large-bore cannulae are better than one 20 gauge in the back of the hand, which is what the crew left her with. If peripheral access fails in a shut-down patient, go intraosseous rather than spending five minutes on a third attempt.
case_actions.prompt_removed_note: Prompted in an earlier draft. Removed because the presentation phase authored nine prompts against a cap of three, which suppressed the antibiotic and the glucocorticoid prompts and left the 240 second deterioration unwarned. The three that survive are the ones prompt_cap_recommendation always named. This action remains critical and a miss is still an omission in the debrief.

case_actions.debrief_note: Appropriate. Two points of access lets the crystalloid and the antibiotic run at the same time rather than in sequence, which in a case measured in minutes is the difference between them.

A good answer to failed peripheral access in a peripherally shut-down patient, and much faster than a central line. Everything in this case can be given intraosseously, including the cephalosporin and the vasopressor. It is not the first choice in a patient who has a usable vein.

Standard. In this patient it is also doing specific work: her potassium is 5.4 and rising along the deterioration branches, so continuous rhythm monitoring is how a peaked T wave or a widening QRS gets noticed before it becomes an arrhythmia.

tag.when: phase is adrenal_crisis OR phase is progressive_meningococcaemia OR phase is frank_septic_shock

case_actions.debrief_note: Reasonable in vasopressor-dependent shock, and it must not delay the vasopressor. Peripheral norepinephrine through a proximal cannula while central access is arranged is accepted practice and the published extravasation rates from short peripheral courses are low, though those series are observational. The wrong order is to leave a patient with a mean arterial pressure in the fifties while a line is placed.

tag.when: phase is adrenal_crisis OR phase is progressive_meningococcaemia OR phase is frank_septic_shock

case_actions.debrief_note: Useful once a vasopressor is titrating, both for beat-to-beat pressure and because this patient needs repeated blood sampling. It is not a priority in the first ten minutes and it should not delay anything. Note the coagulopathy: an arterial puncture in a patient with a falling platelet count and a rising INR is not free.

Her saturation is 98 percent on room air. Oxygen treats hypoxaemia, and she does not have any. The tachypnoea is respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not a failure of oxygenation, and no amount of oxygen will change it. Harmless in itself, and worth naming because it is a reflex that substitutes for looking at the number.
Same error as the nasal cannula, with more theatre. Fifteen litres through a reservoir mask in a patient saturating 98 percent on air treats the observer rather than the patient.

tag.when: phase is improving OR phase is stabilized_shock

case_actions.debrief_note: Not required and not harmless. She is maintaining her own airway, saturating 98 percent on room air, and her tachypnoea is compensating for a metabolic acidosis: paralysing her removes that compensation and the pH falls further. If you intubate, everything that makes this patient fragile arrives at once. Induction agents vasodilate, positive pressure reduces venous return, and she is vasoplegic, volume depleted and unable to mount a cortisol response. That is the physiology of the frank shock phase in this case, and it was avoidable rather than unlucky. When intubation is genuinely needed, the order is: volume in, vasopressor running or drawn up, hydrocortisone given, reduced-dose induction agent, and someone watching the pressure rather than the tube.

prerequisites.when: flag sedation_given set AND flag paralytic_given set
prerequisites.failure_message: She isn't sedated or paralysed yet. We need an induction agent and a paralytic before we tube her.

references: Heffner AC, et al. Predictors of the complication of postintubation hypotension during emergency airway management. J Crit Care. 2012;27(6):587-93. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

case_actions.debrief_note: The single most instructive drug choice in this case. Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, the final enzymatic step in cortisol synthesis, and a single induction dose produces measurable adrenal suppression for 24 to 48 hours. In most patients that is a debating point. In a patient whose adrenal glands have infarcted and who is already glucocorticoid deficient, you are blocking a pathway that has already failed, and the reason it is not tagged harmful is that the outcome evidence in septic shock is contested rather than that the pharmacology is in doubt. If you must intubate her, ketamine at a reduced dose is the better choice, and either way she needs hydrocortisone.
references: Annane D. ICU physicians should abandon the use of etomidate! Intensive Care Med. 2005;31(3):325-6. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

Bruder EA, et al. Single induction dose of etomidate versus other induction agents for endotracheal intubation in critically ill patients. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015. [UNVERIFIED, confirm before release]

case_actions.debrief_note: The better induction agent here if you are intubating. It has no effect on steroidogenesis and its indirect sympathomimetic action is usually helpful in shock. Two caveats worth teaching: that sympathomimetic effect depends on endogenous catecholamine reserve, and in a patient who cannot make cortisol the vascular response to her own catecholamines is already blunted, so reduce the dose and expect less benefit than usual.

The least forgiving induction agent in this physiology. Dose-dependent vasodilation and myocardial depression in a patient who is vasoplegic, preload dependent and unable to mount a stress response. A substantially reduced dose with a vasopressor already running is defensible; a standard induction dose is how a mean arterial pressure of 70 becomes 40.
Slow in onset, unpredictable in effect and hypotensive in shock. It is a poor induction agent generally and a worse one here.

The appropriate paralytic in this patient, specifically because it avoids the potassium rise that succinylcholine causes. Her potassium is 5.4 before you start. The long duration is the trade, and it is why post-intubation sedation is enforced as a follow-up.

Avoidable here. Succinylcholine raises serum potassium by roughly 0.5 mEq/L in normal physiology, and her potassium is already 5.4 and rising as the adrenal crisis progresses. That is not an absolute contraindication, which belongs to the up-regulated receptor states such as burns beyond 24 hours, denervation and prolonged immobility, but rocuronium removes the question entirely and there is no reason to take the risk.

case_actions.debrief_note: A reasonable post-intubation sedative in shock, and it satisfies the sedation obligation without worsening the pressure.

case_actions.debrief_note: Analgesia is a separate requirement from sedation, and in this patient it has a second use: the myalgia is severe and it is one of the things she will remember. Fentanyl is haemodynamically the most forgiving of the opioids, and it does not fix the tube-related distress on its own, so it belongs alongside sedation rather than instead of it.

case_actions.debrief_note: The correct first haemodynamic move and the one this patient needs before any vasopressor. The target is at least 30 mL/kg, which at 62 kg is a little under two litres, given as boluses with reassessment between them rather than as a single number to hit blindly. Two details this case cares about. A balanced crystalloid is preferable to 0.9 percent sodium chloride here, because she already has a metabolic acidosis with a bicarbonate of 19 and a chloride load will not help it; the catalog treats the four crystalloid boluses as interchangeable, so this note covers all of them and the preference has to be taught rather than scored. And a single 500 mL bag is not a resuscitation: it counts as a bolus in this simulator because the catalog groups it with the others, but it is not 30 mL/kg and the debrief will not tell you that unless you read this. Volume alone will not fix her, which is the point of the adrenal crisis branch.

This action deliberately does not satisfy the volume resuscitation requirement in this case: an infusion at a maintenance rate delivers in an hour what she needs in the next ten minutes.
As for the saline infusion: appropriate as continuing fluid, not a substitute for bolus resuscitation, and the balanced composition is preferable in a patient with a metabolic acidosis.

case_actions.debrief_note: Correct treatment for a documented glucose of 53 in a symptomatic patient, and it is symptomatic treatment only. This is the trap the case is built around: dextrose corrects the number for twenty minutes and the glucose falls again, because the reason she is hypoglycaemic is that she has no cortisol. Give the dextrose and give the hydrocortisone. If you gave dextrose and stopped there, the adrenal crisis branch is what that decision looks like. One practical note: 25 grams of 50 percent dextrose is a large, sclerosant, concentrated bolus, and 10 percent dextrose titrated to effect is gentler and increasingly preferred in an alert patient. The catalog has no D10 entry, which is recorded as a change request.

Same caveat as the concentrated bolus: the definitive treatment for this patient's hypoglycaemia is glucocorticoid replacement.

case_actions.debrief_note: Glucagon works by mobilising hepatic glycogen, and it is a reasonable rescue when there is no intravenous access. She has access, so dextrose is faster and more reliable. In a young adult who has been vomiting and not eating for a day, glycogen stores are also depleted, which makes glucagon a weaker choice than it looks.

This is the action the case exists to teach, and it is the one most often missed. Fulminant meningococcaemia can infarct both adrenal glands, and the resulting acute primary adrenal insufficiency produces exactly the biochemistry in front of you: sodium 128, potassium 5.4, glucose 53, and shock that responds poorly to volume and poorly to catecholamines. Glucocorticoid is permissive for the vascular response to catecholamines, which is why a patient in adrenal crisis can be resistant to a vasopressor until she is replaced. Hydrocortisone is the drug rather than another steroid because at stress doses it has meaningful mineralocorticoid activity, which is what the hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia need. The usual adult regimen is 100 mg intravenously followed by 200 mg over 24 hours, by infusion or in divided doses. Do not wait for a cortisol level: in suspected crisis you treat and confirm afterwards, and in this hospital the assay would not return inside this encounter anyway.

The single action with the largest effect on this patient's outcome, and the one that must not wait for anything. A third-generation cephalosporin is the treatment of choice for invasive meningococcal disease and it should be given on clinical suspicion, ideally within an hour of recognising septic shock, and before imaging, before the lumbar puncture, and before any confirmatory test. Two grams intravenously is the meningitis-range dose and is the right empiric choice while meningitis is still on the table. A useful secondary property: ceftriaxone reliably eradicates nasopharyngeal carriage, so the index patient needs no separate carriage-eradication course before discharge, which is not true of most other agents.

case_actions.debrief_note: The correct vasopressor and the correct second step, in that order. Norepinephrine is recommended as the first-line agent in septic shock over dopamine, epinephrine and vasopressin, titrated to a mean arterial pressure of 65. The sequencing is what this case scores: it is indicated once hypotension persists after adequate volume, and starting it in the presentation phase, when she has a systolic pressure of 99 and has had no fluid at all, is treating the monitor rather than the patient. It is also discouraged once she is responding without it. One piece of physiology specific to this case: if she is in adrenal crisis, her vascular response to any catecholamine is blunted until glucocorticoid is replaced, so a rising norepinephrine requirement in a patient with sodium 128, potassium 5.4 and glucose 53 should make you reach for hydrocortisone rather than for a higher rate.

case_actions.debrief_note: Two numbers on the same panel, and this action reads one of them. Her potassium is 5.4, which invites the standard hyperkalaemia bundle. Her glucose on the same panel is 53. Insulin given to shift potassium into cells in a patient who is already hypoglycaemic and cannot mount a counter-regulatory cortisol or glycogenolytic response produces a profound, prolonged hypoglycaemia, and the sedating effect of the shock state means nobody will notice until she seizes or arrests. Two further points worth teaching. Her hyperkalaemia is mineralocorticoid deficiency, and the treatment for it is hydrocortisone and volume, not a potassium-shifting bundle. And a potassium of 5.4 with a normal ECG and no widening does not need emergency shifting at all.

case_actions.debrief_note: Her sodium is 128, and the reason matters more than the number. This is hypovolaemic hyponatraemia from mineralocorticoid deficiency and vomiting, developing over roughly a day, in a patient with no seizures and no signs of cerebral oedema. case_actions.debrief_note: A coagulation panel showing disseminated intravascular coagulation is a description of her sepsis, not an indication to anticoagulate. Her phenotype is consumptive and heading toward bleeding: platelets 110 and falling, INR 1.3 and rising, D-dimer markedly raised, fibrinogen still normal only because it has not been consumed yet. The treatment is the antibiotic and the restoration of perfusion. Therapeutic anticoagulation in sepsis-associated coagulopathy is reserved for overt macrovascular thrombosis and remains genuinely contested between the ISTH, Japanese and North American positions, which is why this is tagged discouraged rather than harmful. Prophylactic-dose venous thromboembolism prevention is a different question and is usually deferred while the platelet count is falling.

Latex agglutination antigen detection for Neisseria meningitidis performs poorly, particularly on urine, and a negative result has no useful negative predictive value in a patient who looks like this. The danger is not the test, it is what a negative result does to a resident who was on the point of giving the right antibiotic. Order it if you like; do not let it into the decision.

No indication. She has vomited twice and has no obstruction, no ileus and no need for gastric decompression or enteral access, and a tube in a coagulopathic patient with a falling platelet count risks epistaxis you will then have to manage. If the aim was to give oral steroid, give intravenous hydrocortisone instead.

Droplet precautions until she has completed 24 hours of effective therapy. This is graded critical for two reasons. The first is that every person in this room is being exposed while it is not done, and the resident is the only one who can order it early enough for that to matter. The second is that anyone exposed to her respiratory secretions before precautions were in place, in particular whoever manages her airway or suctions her without a mask, meets the CDC definition of a close contact and needs chemoprophylaxis themselves. Ordering isolation late is not the same as ordering it.

case_actions.debrief_note: A mask, and eye protection if you are going anywhere near her airway. Meningococcus is transmitted by respiratory droplets and the exposures that produce secondary cases in staff are the airway ones: intubation, suctioning, close bag-mask ventilation. This is the individual half of the same action as the isolation order, and doing it does not substitute for putting the patient on precautions, because that is what protects everyone who comes in after you.

Invasive meningococcal disease is notifiable in every United States jurisdiction, and the notification is what starts contact tracing. Notify on clinical suspicion, not on the culture: chemoprophylaxis is most effective given within 24 hours of identifying the case and is of little or no benefit beyond 14 days. Close contacts means household members, childcare contacts, and anyone directly exposed to her oral secretions in the seven days before onset, which for a student in a shared hall of residence is a specific and identifiable list, plus any staff member who managed her airway unmasked. It does not mean everyone in the waiting room, and nasopharyngeal cultures are not useful for deciding who needs prophylaxis. First-line agents are rifampin, ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone, with azithromycin as an option, and ciprofloxacin should be avoided in areas with documented ciprofloxacin-resistant strains, where CDC advises preferring one of the others. Two further tasks belong to this call: serogroup determination, because a serogroup B case in a vaccinated student raises the question of whether her contacts need a serogroup B vaccine as well as antibiotics, and whether this is part of a cluster on that campus. Do not defer any of it to the admitting team. The emergency department is where the suspicion was raised.

case_actions.debrief_note: The panel that carries the second diagnosis. Read the three together rather than one at a time: sodium 128, potassium 5.4, glucose 53. Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in a shocked patient is mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency, and in fulminant meningococcaemia the mechanism is adrenal haemorrhage. Each number alone has a dozen explanations; together in this context they have one. The creatinine of 1.6 is the third finding: in a 21 year old woman whose baseline would be expected around 0.6 to 0.8, that is a two-fold rise or more, and the bicarbonate of 19 with the raised lactate completes the picture of hypoperfusion.

case_actions.debrief_note: A perfusion measure and, more usefully here, a trend. Ordered once on arrival it reads 2.8 and tells you she is hypoperfused despite a normal blood pressure, which is the point: a systolic of 99 in a 21 year old is not reassurance. Guiding resuscitation by lactate clearance requires re-drawing it, and a lactate that is still climbing after volume is the signal to look for the deficit you have not replaced.

Two sets from separate sites, and the rule that matters more than the drawing is the priority: cultures are obtained if they do not delay the antibiotic, and never instead of it. A single dose of ceftriaxone can sterilise meningococcal blood cultures within an hour, which is exactly why pre-treatment cultures matter for the organism, the serogroup and the susceptibilities, and also exactly why they must not become the reason the antibiotic waited. If the access is difficult, give the drug and draw afterwards. Be honest with learners about what this simulator can and cannot show: cultures take 24 to 48 hours, the five-second laboratory turnaround here cannot represent that, and the result you will see says pending. The organism is not going to be handed to you during this encounter.

case_actions.debrief_note: Indicated in this patient and only while she is haemodynamically stable, which is the discrimination the case is testing. On arrival she has a systolic pressure of 99, she is alert, her platelets are 110 and her INR is 1.3, and a lumbar puncture is reasonable and useful: it is how you establish whether there is meningitis alongside the bacteraemia, which changes treatment duration and the dexamethasone question. Once she is hypotensive it is contraindicated, for three separate reasons that a resident should be able to list: positioning a shocked patient laterally or seated is itself dangerous, the coagulopathy raises the risk of a spinal epidural haematoma as the platelet count falls and the INR rises, and the procedure takes the clinician's attention away from a patient who needs it elsewhere. The prerequisite in this case blocks it in the hypotensive phases and tells you why, because the blocked attempt is the teaching. The rule that never changes: antibiotics do not wait for cerebrospinal fluid. The Gram stain and cell count stay informative for hours after the first dose, and the mortality cost of delay is measured per hour.

A normal cerebrospinal fluid does not downgrade this patient in any way.

case_actions.debrief_note: An underused test and the only one in this catalog that can hand you the organism inside this encounter. Gram stain and culture of a punch biopsy or aspirate of a purpuric lesion demonstrates Gram-negative diplococci in a substantial proportion of cases, and unlike blood cultures it frequently stays positive for some hours after the first antibiotic dose. It confirms a diagnosis you should already be treating: do not wait for it, and do not treat a negative result as reassurance.

Leucocytosis of 18 with a left shift, and the number to watch is the platelet count. One hundred and ten is mildly low on arrival and falls to 75 and then to 55 along the deterioration branches, and a falling platelet count in this presentation is the earliest laboratory sign that the coagulopathy is progressing. Note what a normal or low white count would mean: leucopenia is equally consistent with fulminant meningococcaemia and is a worse prognostic sign, so a reassuring-looking white count is not reassurance.

Mildly prolonged times with a normal fibrinogen on arrival, which is early consumptive coagulopathy before the fibrinogen has been consumed. The trap is reading a normal fibrinogen as evidence against disseminated intravascular coagulation. Fibrinogen is an acute phase reactant, it rises in sepsis, and a normal value in a septic patient can represent a substantial fall from what it should be. The trend matters more than the value, which is why this panel is worth repeating.

Markedly raised, and appropriate to send in this context rather than as a rule-out. In a patient with fever, shock and a petechial rash the D-dimer is part of a coagulopathy panel, not a pulmonary embolism test, and using it as the latter in a patient with a raised D-dimer that was never going to be negative is how an unnecessary CT pulmonary angiogram gets ordered.

The fastest useful test in the first two minutes. A pH of 7.31 with a bicarbonate of 19 and a venous pCO2 of 32 is a metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation, which is what her respiratory rate of 24 is for. Two things follow. Her tachypnoea is not a lung problem and does not need oxygen. And if you paralyse her, you remove the compensation, and the pH falls.

More useful here than it looks, because it settles the one differential that would send this patient down an entirely different pathway. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura gives a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes and a normal coagulation profile; this film shows toxic granulation and left shift with no schistocytes, alongside a raised INR and a raised D-dimer. That combination is consumptive coagulopathy, not a microangiopathy, and it means antibiotics rather than plasma exchange.
Markedly raised, confirmatory of something you already know, and it must never be the test that decides whether this patient gets an antibiotic. Ordering it is not wrong. Waiting for it is.
Raised and non-specific. It has a place in following a treated infection over days and none in the next twenty minutes.

Mild transaminase rise and a marginally raised bilirubin, which is hypoperfusion and sepsis rather than a hepatic problem in its own right. Worth having on the admission problem list, not worth acting on here.

Concentrated with granular casts and no evidence of infection: negative nitrite, negative leucocyte esterase, no bacteria. Two useful things. The granular casts with an otherwise bland sediment fit acute tubular injury from hypoperfusion, which is what her creatinine of 1.6 is. And the negative infection markers remove the urinary tract as the source, which in a young woman with fever and shock is the source most often assumed without being checked.

Reasonable to send in a febrile young adult in season, and a positive result would not change what she needs. The reason influenza appears on the differential at all is that the first hours of meningococcal disease are genuinely indistinguishable from it: fever, myalgia, headache, malaise. The discriminators are the ones she has, which are the non-blanching rash, the cold peripheries with a normal pressure, and the biochemistry. Anchoring on a positive influenza test in a patient with purpura is a recognised route to a missed meningococcal death.

Appropriate for admission and infection-control purposes and irrelevant to the decisions in front of you. Note that it is a nasopharyngeal swab, so it is an aerosol-adjacent procedure that should happen after droplet precautions are in place, not before.

Two questions, both worth asking. Is this rhythm sinus tachycardia or an arrhythmia, because the answer determines whether rate control is even a candidate: it is sinus at 124, so it is not. And does a potassium of 5.4 have electrocardiographic consequences, because that determines whether the hyperkalaemia needs emergency treatment: here there is no peaking, no QRS widening and no loss of P waves, so it does not. An ECG that answers two management questions in ten seconds is a good use of ten seconds.

Normal, and worth having. It excludes the alternative sources for a septic young adult that would change antibiotics, particularly a lobar pneumonia, and it gives you a baseline film. Note the result-freezing behaviour in this simulator: a film ordered before intubation will not show an endotracheal tube even if it arrives afterwards.

Mandatory in a 21 year old woman, and not because pregnancy is likely here. It is negative. The reason to send it is that a positive result changes the differential substantially, changes the imaging you are willing to do, and changes several drug choices, and none of those decisions can be unmade later. Note the catalog's own warning about this study: its default result asserts that an unauthored patient is not pregnant, which is a silent assumption rather than a normal value.
Negative. Reasonable if you want a definitive answer rather than a bedside one, and the urine test answers the question fast enough for these decisions.
Sensible forward planning in a patient with a falling platelet count and a coagulopathy who may need product later. It is not a decision-making test now.

Useful and quick. In this patient it does two things: it shows a hyperdynamic, underfilled left ventricle with a collapsing inferior vena cava, which supports volume as the first intervention and argues against a cardiogenic cause for the shock, and it excludes a pericardial effusion. Septic cardiomyopathy can appear later in the illness; it is not what is happening at this point.

Reasonable if you are worried about an obstructive cause for the creatinine of 1.6, and there is nothing in the history to suggest one. Normal here. Her acute kidney injury is prerenal and septic, and the treatment is perfusion.

Appropriate in a shocked patient with an acute kidney injury. Hourly urine output is the cheapest continuous measure of renal perfusion available and it is one of the two KDIGO criteria; in the first hours it is the more useful of the two, because creatinine lags the injury by a day or more and will not fall during this encounter however well you resuscitate. Weigh the catheter-associated infection risk, which here is easily outweighed.

The right antipyretic and analgesic for this patient, chosen by exclusion: it is neither nephrotoxic in a kidney that has already been injured nor antiplatelet in a patient with a consumptive coagulopathy. Fever raises metabolic demand in a patient whose oxygen delivery is already inadequate, and her myalgia is genuinely severe. The evidence that antipyresis improves outcome in sepsis is weak; the argument here is comfort and demand reduction at very low cost.

Reasonable. She has vomited twice and cannot keep fluid down, which is part of why she is volume depleted and hyponatraemic. Low cost, and it does not substitute for the intravenous route for anything that matters.

A patient with vasopressor-dependent or vasopressor-threatening septic shock, an acute kidney injury, a consumptive coagulopathy and an endocrine emergency needs an intensive care bed, and bed allocation is usually the rate-limiting step in the department. Call early. The referral should carry five things: the antibiotic and its timing, that hydrocortisone has been given and why, the vasopressor and its trend, that this is a notifiable disease with contact tracing under way, and the platelet and coagulation trend. If you have not given hydrocortisone, expect the intensivist to ask about it before anything else.

case_actions.debrief_note: Useful and not required from the emergency department. Infectious diseases will handle narrowing therapy once the isolate returns, treatment duration, serogroup determination, and the vaccination conversation this patient specifically needs, which is that a serogroup B case in a student who received the routine conjugate vaccine is exactly what the conjugate vaccine does not cover. They will usually coordinate with public health, and that does not discharge your own obligation to notify. Do not let waiting for them delay the first antibiotic dose.

Appropriate, and after the hydrocortisone rather than before it. Endocrinology will confirm the diagnosis properly with a cortisol and ACTH once she is stable, plan the taper and the transition to oral replacement, decide whether she needs fludrocortisone, and organise the education and emergency injection kit that a patient with new adrenal insufficiency must not leave hospital without. The important point about sequencing: in suspected adrenal crisis you treat first and confirm afterwards, and if a stimulation test is planned later, that is the one situation in which dexamethasone is preferred over hydrocortisone because it does not cross-react with the cortisol assay.

Not needed from the emergency department. A creatinine of 1.6 in a septic, hypovolaemic 21 year old is prerenal and septic acute tubular injury, and the treatment is the treatment of the shock. There is no dialysis indication: no refractory acidosis, no refractory hyperkalaemia, no uraemic complication, no diuretic-refractory overload. What the call usually signals is that the creatinine was read as a kidney problem rather than as a perfusion problem seen through the kidney. Worth doing instead: stop the nephrotoxins, keep the mean arterial pressure up, and measure the urine output.

Reasonable but not urgent, and the answer will be that the coagulopathy is a consequence of the sepsis and its treatment is the treatment of the sepsis. Haematology becomes genuinely useful if she bleeds, if the purpura becomes fulminant with threatened limbs, where protein C replacement has been described, or if a microangiopathy cannot be excluded on the film.

No focal deficit, no seizure, supple neck, normal cerebrospinal fluid where it was obtained. Her altered mental state is a perfusion and metabolic problem, specifically hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hypoperfusion, and it improves as those are treated. Nothing here needs a neurologist.
Completion of the case. Disposition and diagnosis are scored separately; see the handoff section.

In a patient this unwell the airway question is answered by listening to her talk, and she is talking. Patent, protecting it, speaking in sentences even if slowly. This is the finding that says she does not need a tube, which matters in a case where intubating her is the route to the worst phase.

Tachypnoeic with no increased work of breathing, which is a specific and important combination. A patient who is breathing fast without pulling with her accessory muscles and without hypoxaemia is compensating for a metabolic acidosis, not failing to oxygenate. Recognising that stops you treating her lungs.

The manoeuvre that reveals this case. Her blood pressure is 99 over 63 and normal for her age, and her hands are cold to the wrist with a capillary refill of three seconds and thready peripheral pulses. That is compensated shock: a young patient maintains her pressure by clamping down until she cannot, and by the time the number falls she has been shocked for some time. Perfusion is this examination, not the monitor.

Dry mucous membranes supporting the volume depletion, and a specific negative that earns its place: fundoscopy is normal with no papilloedema. That is one of the findings whose absence removes the indication for a CT head before a lumbar puncture. No conjunctival petechiae, and no oropharyngeal exudate.

Supple, with no meningism. Kernig and Brudzinski are negative and she moves her neck freely on request. This is the most important pertinent negative in the case: invasive meningococcal disease does not require meningitis, the purely septicaemic form carries the higher mortality, and waiting for a stiff neck before treating gets the sicker end of the spectrum treated later. Jugular venous pressure is low, consistent with hypovolaemia.

Tachycardic and regular with normal heart sounds, no murmur and no gallop, and no peripheral oedema. All negatives, and useful ones: they argue against endocarditis with septic emboli, which is on the differential for fever with a petechial rash, and against a cardiogenic contribution to the shock.
Clear and equal throughout with good air entry and no crackles. That removes pneumonia as the source in a septic young adult, which is the commonest source and therefore the one most often assumed.

Soft and non-tender with no organomegaly and normal bowel sounds. A negative that matters twice: it moves an intra-abdominal source down the list in a patient who has been vomiting, and there is no hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases or scars, which is what you would look for if you were thinking of chronic rather than acute adrenal insufficiency. This crisis is days old, not years, so the skin has had no time to change.

Authored specifically as a pertinent negative, and it is the one that excludes the differential most easily missed in a 21 year old woman with fever, a rash and hypotension. There is no retained tampon, no vaginal foreign body, no discharge and no adnexal tenderness. Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome presents exactly this way and the source is often a tampon, a nasal pack or a wound, so the examination that excludes it is not optional. Note that her rash is petechial and purpuric rather than the diffuse macular erythroderma of toxic shock, which is the other discriminator.
No costovertebral angle tenderness, which alongside the bland urinalysis removes pyelonephritis as the source. No spinal tenderness and no rash over the back at this stage.

Severe symmetrical myalgia in the thighs and calves, tender to squeeze, with full passive movement, soft compartments and intact distal neurovascular status. The myalgia is not incidental. Severe limb pain, cold hands and feet and abnormal skin colour are described as early features of meningococcal sepsis appearing before the rash and before any meningism, and a patient who cannot stand because her legs hurt this much is giving you information. That literature is largely paediatric and its generalisation to a 21 year old is not established, so treat it as a pattern worth recognising rather than a validated rule.

The finding that makes the diagnosis. Non-blanching petechiae on both ankles and feet on arrival, spreading and coalescing into purpura along the deterioration branches. Two techniques worth teaching because they take four seconds: press the lesion and watch whether it blanches, and press a glass slide over it if you are unsure. A non-blanching rash with fever and shock is invasive meningococcal disease until proven otherwise. She is also diaphoretic and mottled peripherally, and there is no hyperpigmentation, no target lesions, no vesicles and no eschar.

Mental status is a perfusion and metabolic measurement, and here it is doing both jobs. On arrival she is GCS 15 but slow, which is more than her observed vital signs would explain and is partly a glucose of 53. She becomes drowsy in the deterioration phases and obtunded after intubation. No focal deficit, no papilloedema, no meningism: the combination that says a CT head before a lumbar puncture is not indicated.

Anxious, frightened and cooperative, with linear thought. Recording it matters because it is the baseline against which the later change in her mental state is judged, and because agitation and confusion in a young patient with fever are too easily attributed to something behavioural.

follow_ups.applies_when: flag dextrose_given set AND NOT flag steroid_given set
follow_ups.nurse_prompt: Do you want me to recheck her sugar? It's been a couple of minutes since the dextrose.
follow_ups.debrief_note: This is the follow-up that carries the case's central lesson, and its condition does real work: it applies only while dextrose has been given and glucocorticoid has not. A glucose that falls again after correction is not a dosing problem, it is a hormonal one, and rechecking is how you find that out. Note that giving hydrocortisone also discharges this obligation, because at that point the underlying deficit has been treated.

follow_ups.applies_when: flag fluids_given set AND flag lactate_sent set
follow_ups.nurse_prompt: She's had the fluid. Do you want another lactate to see where she is?
follow_ups.debrief_note: Lactate clearance, not a single lactate, is what guides resuscitation. Because results in this simulator freeze at the state in which they were ordered, the only way to see a trend is to order it again. A lactate that has not fallen after adequate volume is the prompt to ask what deficit remains, and in this patient the answer is cortisol.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: She hasn't passed urine since she got here, and her roommate said not since last night. Do you want a catheter so we can measure it?
follow_ups.debrief_note: Urine output is the earliest available measure of the renal response to resuscitation and one of the two KDIGO criteria for acute kidney injury. It matters more than the creatinine in the first hours, because creatinine lags the injury by a day or more and will not improve during this encounter.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: She's in droplet precautions now. Do you want us all masked up in here?
follow_ups.debrief_note: Ordering precautions and complying with them are different acts, and the second is the one that protects the people at the head of the bed. Anyone exposed to her respiratory secretions before a mask went on is a close contact by the CDC definition and needs chemoprophylaxis.

follow_ups.applies_when: flag isolation_precautions set AND NOT flag public_health_notified set
follow_ups.nurse_prompt: If we're isolating her for this, does the health department need to know tonight?
follow_ups.debrief_note: The obligation is created by the suspicion, not by the culture. Notify so that contact tracing starts inside the 24 hour window in which chemoprophylaxis is most effective. A resident who isolates the patient but does not notify has protected this room and nobody in her hall of residence.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: She's tubed and still paralysed from the roc. Do you want something written up for sedation and pain?
follow_ups.debrief_note: A paralysed patient without sedation is awake, aware and unable to signal. This obligation is created by the intubation and cannot precede it, which is why it is a follow-up rather than a prerequisite. Choose the agent with the blood pressure in mind: propofol in a patient who is already hypotensive will make it worse.

follow_ups.nurse_prompt: Do you want a film to check the tube? Anything you ordered before we tubed her won't show it.
follow_ups.debrief_note: Radiographic confirmation of tube depth is standard and does not replace waveform capnography, which is what confirms tracheal placement. The simulator detail matters: results freeze at the state in which they were ordered, so a film requested before intubation will not show the tube, and a repeat order is needed.

prompt_cap_recommendation.rationale: The presentation phase originally carried nine prompts against a cap of three, so the antibiotic and the glucocorticoid were suppressed and the 240 second deterioration fired with neither warned. Prompts are now authored only on the three actions listed below plus the vasopressor and the intensive care referral, which are critical in later phases where they do not compete. The loss is real and accepted: the isolation order and the public health call are critical and now unprompted, and both are surfaced as omissions in the debrief instead.

prerequisite_semantics_note: Prerequisite 'when' states the condition that MUST BE TRUE for the action to proceed, matching the worked table in section 8.1. The failure message is shown when it evaluates false.

exam.authoring_note: Bound to the action catalog's closed set of 14 manoeuvres. Findings are placed by the catalog's exam_finding_routing map rather than by preference: capillary refill, skin temperature and pulse quality under the circulation exam; the rash and diaphoresis under the skin exam; level of consciousness under the neurological exam; limb pain, compartments and distal neurovascular status under the musculoskeletal exam; work of breathing under the breathing exam; fundoscopy under HEENT; costovertebral angle tenderness under the back exam; jugular venous pressure and tracheal position under the neck exam. All 14 are authored, including exam_gu, which exists solely to carry the pertinent negative that excludes toxic shock syndrome.

value.findings: Endotracheal tube in place and secured, cuff inflated. Airway protected by the tube. Scant clear secretions.
Endotracheal tube in place and secured, cuff inflated. Airway protected by the tube.
Airway patent and self-maintained. No stridor, no drooling, no oropharyngeal swelling. She is speaking in full sentences, slowly, and stops between them.

If you are ringing me about a shocked young adult with non-blanching purpura, the answer is that she needs two grams of ceftriaxone before we discuss anything else, and we can talk about the rest afterwards."

consult_endocrinology.when: (phase is improving OR phase is stabilized_shock) AND flag steroid_given set
consult_endocrinology.value: Endocrinology: "Her numbers are moving in the right direction, which is what replacement does and is itself supportive of the diagnosis. Keep the hydrocortisone going at 200 milligrams over 24 hours rather than stopping after one dose, because the deficit has not gone away. She does not need fludrocortisone while she is on that much hydrocortisone. A cortisol drawn before you replaced her would have been worth having and one drawn now will not be interpretable, so do not chase it tonight. Adrenal imaging, education, an emergency injection kit and a steroid card all belong to the admission."

consult_endocrinology.when: flag steroid_given set AND study basic_chemistry_chem_7 resulted
consult_endocrinology.value: Endocrinology: "Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia with shock in a previously well 21 year old, and you have given hydrocortisone. That is the right order: in suspected adrenal crisis you treat and confirm afterwards, and if this is meningococcal sepsis the mechanism is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage. Keep going with 200 milligrams over 24 hours rather than one dose. She does not need fludrocortisone while she is on that much hydrocortisone, because at stress doses it has enough mineralocorticoid activity of its own. Save a serum sample now if you can, since a cortisol drawn before replacement is worth having and ours will not return tonight. She will need imaging of the adrenals, education, an emergency injection kit and a steroid card before she goes home, and none of that is tonight's problem."

consult_endocrinology.when: study basic_chemistry_chem_7 resulted AND NOT flag steroid_given set
consult_endocrinology.value: Endocrinology: "Read those three results together rather than one at a time. A low sodium, a raised potassium and a glucose below 70, in a shocked 21 year old with no diabetes and no diuretic. That is combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid failure, and with a purpuric rash the mechanism is adrenal haemorrhage. Give 100 milligrams of hydrocortisone intravenously now. Do not wait for a cortisol level and do not give dexamethasone instead unless you are planning a stimulation test, because it has no mineralocorticoid activity and her sodium and potassium need that."

consult_endocrinology.when: study basic_chemistry_chem_7 ordered AND NOT study basic_chemistry_chem_7 resulted
consult_endocrinology.value: Endocrinology: "I cannot say anything useful until that panel is back. Three numbers decide this: sodium, potassium and glucose. Ring me the moment you have them. If her sugar is low and you have a bedside reading already, tell me that now."

Endocrinology: "A glucose that low in a 21 year old who is not diabetic and has taken no insulin needs an explanation, and in a shocked febrile patient the explanation to exclude first is that she has no cortisol. Send a full chemistry panel and look specifically at the sodium and potassium. If they are low and high respectively, treat her."

Endocrinology: "Tell me her sodium, her potassium and her glucose, and whether she is hypotensive. Those four things decide whether this is an adrenal crisis. Send a chemistry panel and a bedside sugar and call me back."

consult_public_health_authorities.when: flag isolation_precautions set AND flag abx_given set
consult_public_health_authorities.value: Communicable disease duty officer: "Thank you for calling tonight rather than tomorrow. Taking the details now. She is in droplet precautions and has had ceftriaxone, which is what we want, and because it was ceftriaxone she does not need a separate course to clear her own carriage before discharge. On the contacts: household members, anyone she has kissed or shared drinks or utensils with, and anyone exposed to her oral secretions in the seven days before she became unwell. For a student in a shared hall that means her room, her immediate suite or floor if they share a kitchen or bathroom, and her partner if she has one. Whole-building prophylaxis is not indicated and we will not be doing it. It also means your own staff: anyone who intubated her, suctioned her or bag-masked her without a mask goes on the list, so please give me those names. We use rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone, azithromycin if needed, and we are avoiding ciprofloxacin in this catchment at the moment because of resistant isolates. Ideally everyone is dosed within 24 hours; after 14 days there is little point. Send me the isolate and the serogroup as soon as you have them, because if this is group B we will be looking at whether her contacts need a group B vaccine as well as antibiotics, and whether there are other cases on that campus."

Communicable disease duty officer: "Noted, and I will start the notification now on clinical suspicion. Two things at your end before I go. Is she in droplet precautions, because she needs to be until she has had 24 hours of treatment, and has anyone had an unprotected airway exposure, because those staff need prophylaxis. On her contacts: household and anyone exposed to her oral secretions in the previous seven days, and for a student that means her room and shared living space rather than the whole hall. Rifampin, ceftriaxone or azithromycin, ideally inside 24 hours. Send me the serogroup when it comes."

Communicable disease duty officer: "I can take this as a suspected case now, and I would rather have it early and be wrong than late and right. Tell me what makes you suspect it and what she has had. Has she had an antibiotic yet, and is she in droplet precautions? Those two answers change what I do at this end. If you have not treated her yet, do that first and call me straight back."

consult_renal.when: study basic_chemistry_chem_7 resulted AND flag steroid_given set
consult_renal.value: Nephrology: "A creatinine in that range in a 21 year old whose baseline would be about 0.7 is a stage 2 injury by the KDIGO ratio, not a mild one, and it is prerenal and septic rather than intrinsic renal disease. No dialysis indication: no refractory acidosis, no refractory hyperkalaemia, no uraemic complication, no fluid-refractory overload. Do the boring things. Keep the mean pressure at 65, get a catheter in and follow hourly output, and keep non-steroidals, contrast and aminoglycosides away from her. Her potassium is an aldosterone problem and it will come down as the hydrocortisone and the volume work; do not reach for insulin and dextrose in a patient who was hypoglycaemic an hour ago. And do not expect the creatinine to fall tonight, because it lags."

Nephrology: "A creatinine well above what a 21 year old should have, with a low bicarbonate and a raised potassium. That is a prerenal and septic acute kidney injury and the treatment is the treatment of her shock. No dialysis indication. Avoid non-steroidals and contrast, measure her urine output. One thing I would say before I hang up: a raised potassium with a low sodium in a shocked young person is a hormone problem, not a renal one, and somebody should be thinking about her adrenals."

consult_renal.when: study basic_chemistry_chem_7 ordered AND NOT study basic_chemistry_chem_7 resulted
consult_renal.value: Nephrology: "Nothing useful from me until the chemistry is back. Send me the creatinine, the potassium and the bicarbonate when they land, and tell me what her urine output has been. Meanwhile keep her pressure up, which is the only thing that will help her kidneys tonight."
Nephrology: "I have no numbers on this patient. Send a chemistry panel and a urinalysis and tell me what she has passed since she arrived, then call me back."

consult_heme_onc.when: study coagulation_panel resulted AND study peripheral_smear resulted
consult_heme_onc.value: Haematology: "Platelets falling, INR up, aPTT up, D-dimer very high, and no schistocytes on the film. That combination is disseminated intravascular coagulation from her sepsis, not a microangiopathy, and the absence of fragments is what rules out thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. So: no plasma exchange, and treat the sepsis, because that is the treatment for the coagulopathy. She is not bleeding, so no platelets and no plasma. Do not anticoagulate her. Watch the fibrinogen rather than the platelet count, because a normal fibrinogen in a septic patient is already a fall. If the purpura starts extending into confluent necrosis with a threatened limb, ring me immediately, because purpura fulminans is a different conversation and protein C replacement has been used in it."

Haematology: "Prolonged times with a raised D-dimer and a falling platelet count in a septic patient is consumptive coagulopathy. Treat the sepsis. She is not bleeding, so hold off on products, and do not anticoagulate. Send me a film, because the one thing I want to exclude is a microangiopathy, and schistocytes are how I do that."

consult_heme_onc.when: study coagulation_panel ordered AND NOT study coagulation_panel resulted
consult_heme_onc.value: Haematology: "Send me the numbers when they arrive, and a fibrinogen with them. Is she actually bleeding anywhere, or are we talking about a rash? If the purpura is spreading while you watch it, say so now, because that changes what I do."
Haematology: "Send a full coagulation screen with a fibrinogen and a D-dimer, and a peripheral film, then call me back. Is she bleeding from anywhere, or is this purpura?"

authoring_notes.alertness_gating: Section 10.5 asks for alertness gating authored once as a global rule. The condition language has no alertness predicate, so the rule enumerates the phases whose alertness level is 2 or 3: frank_septic_shock and halted. A second global rule covers intubation, which is reachable in the improving phase without a phase change. The validator check that every alertness-gated phase appears in the global rule must not be removed, because adding a phase later breaks this silently.
authoring_notes.drowsiness_gating: Section 10.5 also requires a second answer for the phases in which the patient can speak but not fully. Here that is alertness level 1 in adrenal_crisis and progressive_meningococcaemia, where she is drowsy rather than distressed: the answers carry the same fact in fewer words, and she loses detail and dates rather than losing content. This roughly doubles the interview authoring and it is the reason the topic count is what it is.
authoring_notes.diagnosis_disclosure: Section 10.4 forbids the patient from stating or implying the diagnosis. Two places sit close to the line and both are flagged for the reviewing physician. She describes a rash she can see on her own ankles, which is her own observation rather than an interpretation. And on vaccination she says she had 'two of those' meningitis shots without naming a serogroup or connecting them to today, which is what a 21 year old would actually be able to tell you. She never uses the words sepsis, meningitis, meningococcus or adrenal, and she never attributes today's illness to a cause.
authoring_notes.coverage_note: All of the section 10.2 minimum list is authored, including topics this case does not turn on, because with the Patient tab gone an unauthored topic is a dead end rather than an inconvenience. Pregnancy status and menstrual history are authored in full rather than skipped, since the patient is a 21 year old woman and the tampon question is the pertinent negative that excludes toxic shock syndrome.
