correct_disposition.label: Intensive care unit
correct_disposition.explanation: Invasive meningococcal disease with septic shock in a 21 year old, with a progressing consumptive coagulopathy, an acute kidney injury and a new endocrine emergency requiring ongoing intravenous glucocorticoid. She needs continuous haemodynamic monitoring, the ability to start or titrate a vasopressor at short notice, hourly urine output, serial lactate and serial coagulation studies, and droplet precautions maintained until she has had 24 hours of effective therapy. This is true on the path where she never needed a vasopressor as well as on the path where she did: the disease she has can extend purpura and consume platelets over hours, and the unit is where that gets noticed.

alternative_dispositions.label: Step-down or high dependency unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Closer than the ward and still wrong, and the reasoning matters more than the label. Ask what the unit has to be able to do: start a vasopressor within minutes of a pressure falling, recognise purpura extending across a shift, act on a platelet count that has halved. Most step-down units cannot do the first and are not staffed for the second. If she required a vasopressor at any point in this case, this answer is unambiguously wrong.

alternative_dispositions.label: General medical ward with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Telemetry gives you a rhythm, and her rhythm was never the problem. The judgement error here is treating improvement as resolution: she looks much better after antibiotics, hydrocortisone and volume, and she looks better because of three interventions whose effect is measured in hours in a disease that can kill in hours. Fulminant meningococcal disease deteriorating on a general ward is a recognised route to a preventable death.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Observation is for patients with a low probability of a serious outcome and one short question to answer. She has a confirmed shock state, organ dysfunction in two systems, a coagulopathy that is still moving, and a case fatality in the range of 10 to 15 percent even with correct treatment.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home with oral antibiotics and return advice
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Unsafe, and it is on this list because it happens. The first hours of meningococcal disease in a young adult are genuinely indistinguishable from influenza, and students are sent home from urgent care at that stage and found dead. The discriminators are all present here and all available at the bedside within two minutes: a rash that does not blanch, cold peripheries with a normal blood pressure, severe limb pain, and a glucose of 53.

alternative_dispositions.label: Transfer to a tertiary or quaternary centre
alternative_dispositions.explanation: She is already in one. This option is included because transfer is the right answer to this presentation in a critical access hospital, and the point worth taking away is that the correct disposition depends on the care setting, which the case states. Where transfer is genuinely needed, antibiotics, hydrocortisone and resuscitation happen before she moves, never after.

alternative_dispositions.label: Operating room for source control
alternative_dispositions.explanation: There is no surgical source. Choosing this usually means the purpura was read as necrotising soft tissue infection, which is a reasonable thing to consider and is excluded here by the distribution and the character of the lesions: symmetrical non-blanching petechiae and purpura on both ankles progressing centrally, with no pain out of proportion over a single region, no crepitus, no bullae and no rapidly advancing margin in one limb. Debridement of purpura fulminans has a place late in the illness, and it is not an emergency department decision on the day of presentation.

correct_diagnosis.label: Meningococcaemia (invasive Neisseria meningitidis infection) with septic shock
correct_diagnosis.explanation: A previously well 21 year old in a shared hall of residence, with twelve hours of fever, rigors and severe symmetrical limb pain, cold peripheries with a normal blood pressure, and a non-blanching petechial rash appearing on the ankles within hours and spreading. Add an early consumptive coagulopathy, an acute kidney injury, and a serum sodium of 128 with a potassium of 5.4 and a glucose of 53, which is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage complicating the septicaemia. Two features are worth stating explicitly because they are the ones that delay the diagnosis: the neck is supple and the cerebrospinal fluid is normal, and meningococcal disease does not require meningitis; and she is vaccinated, which covers serogroups A, C, W and Y and not B.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Septic shock
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True, and incomplete in a way that matters. Septic shock names the syndrome and not the organism, and here the organism determines the antibiotic, the isolation, the notification and the chemoprophylaxis of everyone on her floor. A resident who stops at septic shock will treat this patient correctly and will not protect her hall of residence. Credit the recognition; push for the organism.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Adrenal crisis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Also true, also incomplete, and the mirror image of the previous answer. She is in adrenal crisis, and it is a complication of the thing that is actually killing her. A resident who reaches this diagnosis has done the harder piece of pattern recognition in this case and must not stop there, because hydrocortisone without ceftriaxone treats the endocrine emergency and leaves the meningococcus running. Note the schema limitation: the handoff accepts one diagnosis, and the honest answer to this case is two.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Bacterial meningitis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The commonest wrong answer, because meningococcus and meningitis are joined in most people's memory. She has no meningitis: her neck is supple, Kernig and Brudzinski are negative, she has no photophobia, and her cerebrospinal fluid has three white cells. Invasive meningococcal disease runs on a spectrum from meningitis without shock to fulminant septicaemia without meningitis, and the purely septicaemic form is the one with the higher mortality. Waiting for meningism before treating selects for treating the sicker patients later.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Toxic shock syndrome
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The differential that most deserves to be actively excluded rather than dismissed, because a 21 year old woman with fever, hypotension, a rash, vomiting, myalgia and confusion is the textbook presentation and the source is often a tampon, a nasal pack or a minor wound. Two things exclude it here, and both require you to have looked: the genital examination shows no retained tampon, no foreign body and no discharge, and the rash is wrong. Toxic shock produces a diffuse blanching macular erythroderma, like sunburn, with desquamation at one to two weeks. Hers is petechial and purpuric and does not blanch.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A genuine mimic and worth carrying, because it is diagnosed clinically, serology is retrospective, and the mortality comes from delayed doxycycline. Against it here: no tick exposure, no outdoor exposure, and a tempo and distribution that do not fit. The rash of spotted fever typically appears around day three to five of illness and begins on the wrists and ankles before spreading centrally; hers appeared within twelve hours of the first symptom. If you had genuinely considered it and added doxycycline, that was cheap and defensible.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She has it, and it is not a diagnosis. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is always secondary, and naming it as the answer stops the search at the complication instead of the cause. The clinical consequence is real: the treatment for her coagulopathy is the antibiotic and the restoration of perfusion, and a resident anchored on the coagulopathy reaches for platelets, plasma or heparin instead.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Purpura fulminans
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A description of what her skin may become rather than a diagnosis of what she has, and it is the same category error as choosing the coagulopathy. Purpura fulminans is worth knowing as the endpoint of this process, driven by acquired protein C deficiency with dermal vessel thrombosis, because it is what threatens her limbs over the next 48 hours. It does not name the organism and it does not trigger the public health response.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Reasonable to raise on fever, thrombocytopenia, altered mentation and an acute kidney injury, which is four of the five classical features, and settled decisively by two results. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a microangiopathy: the film shows schistocytes and the coagulation profile is normal, because platelets are consumed and clotting factors are not. Her film has no schistocytes and her INR, aPTT and D-dimer are all deranged, which is a consumptive coagulopathy. Getting this wrong sends a patient toward plasma exchange instead of antibiotics.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Influenza
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: This is the error that kills people in the first hours of meningococcal disease, and it is on the list for that reason rather than because it is silly. Fever, rigors, severe myalgia, headache and vomiting in a student during influenza season is influenza most of the time. The four discriminators are the rash that does not blanch, the cold peripheries with a normal blood pressure, the severity and distribution of the limb pain, and the biochemistry. Note that a positive influenza antigen test would not change any of that: co-infection exists, and anchoring on a positive result in a patient with purpura is a described route to a missed death.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hypoglycaemia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A finding rather than a diagnosis, and the question it should have raised is why a previously well 21 year old who takes no insulin has a glucose of 53. In this patient the answer is on the same panel, in the sodium and the potassium. Treating the number with dextrose and moving on is precisely the path the case models as the adrenal crisis branch.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Undifferentiated shock
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Defensible for the first ninety seconds and not at handoff. By the time you are handing over you have a fever, a non-blanching rash, a lactate, a chemistry panel and a coagulation screen, and the shock is no longer undifferentiated. Handing over an undifferentiated label to an intensivist loses the two things that change what they do next, which are the organism and the adrenal failure.

alternative_diagnoses.label: IgA vasculitis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A palpable purpuric rash on the lower limbs with arthralgia, abdominal symptoms and renal involvement genuinely overlaps with this presentation, and it is the reason a purpuric rash is sometimes treated as a dermatological problem. What separates them is the systemic state: IgA vasculitis does not produce shock, a lactate of 2.8, a glucose of 53 or a consumptive coagulopathy, and it usually follows an upper respiratory illness by one to two weeks rather than twelve hours.

clinical_domains.label: Recognising and treating the adrenal crisis

cross_cutting_teaching_points: The organising idea in this case is that there are two deficits and they are treated with two different drugs. The antibiotic treats the organism and the hydrocortisone treats the adrenal failure the organism caused, and neither substitutes for the other. The two deterioration branches exist to make that concrete: fix the volume and the glucose without the cortisol and she goes one way, fix the cortisol without the organism and she goes the other.

A normal blood pressure in a 21 year old is not reassurance. Young patients maintain a systolic pressure by vasoconstricting until they cannot, and by the time the number falls they have been shocked for some time. The findings that told you she was shocked on arrival were all at the bedside and free: cold hands with a capillary refill of three seconds, a lactate of 2.8, and no urine since last night.

Read the chemistry panel as a pattern rather than as seven separate results. Sodium 128, potassium 5.4 and glucose 53 each have a dozen explanations alone. Together, in a shocked patient with purpura, they have one, and the diagnosis is made on the panel rather than on any test that confirms it.

Two of the harmful actions in this case are attempts to treat a single abnormal number in isolation: insulin for the potassium of 5.4, and rate control for the tachycardia of 124. Both are lethal here for the same underlying reason, which is that the number was compensation or consequence rather than the disease.

This patient is not the only person affected by what you do. Droplet precautions, personal protective equipment, notification on suspicion, and a contact list that includes her suitemates and any staff member who managed her airway unmasked. Notification is the action with the largest effect on people who are not yet patients, and it is the one most often left to the admitting team.

Be honest with learners about what this simulator could not model. The seed for this case describes a patient who deteriorates when treatment is delayed. This engine has no time-driven transitions, so ignoring every prompt produces the same patient as acting immediately, and the cost of delay appears only in the debrief timings. Outside the simulator, the cost is measured per hour.
debrief_configuration.attempt_history_note: This case is built to be replayed. The two deterioration branches are mutually exclusive within a single run: a resident who gives fluid and dextrose without hydrocortisone never sees the meningococcaemia branch, and one who gives hydrocortisone first never sees the adrenal branch. Seeing both requires two runs, and that is the intended use.
debrief_configuration.trap_actions_note: Plausible-looking actions that are wrong here. All are tagged discouraged rather than neutral, which is the tier v0.4 added for exactly this purpose, so they carry scoring weight as well as a debrief note. Vancomycin is on the list in a qualified sense: it is reasonable empiric practice and it is a trap only if it is the antibiotic a resident believes has treated the meningococcus.
